title: Customer POC RapidStart Tooling and Hands-on Lab
content:
Goal:
This is a lightweight, reproducible RapidStart toolkit for Solutions Engineering POCs. Objective is to run a 90-minute customer lab that proves: (1) Redwood hosted API quick integration, (2) private/VPC deploy skeleton for secure evaluation, (3) a simple cost/latency experiment that demonstrates batching + KV-cache benefits, and (4) graceful fallback to a smaller model during capacity constraints.

Audience:
- Customer engineers (software/ML) evaluating Redwood for production inference.
- SEs running the workshop: bring infra creds and a laptop.

High-level checklist (pre-work for SE):
- [ ] Create small demo project in GitHub (starter repo linked above) and fork per-customer.
- [ ] Provision a short-lived private VPC demo environment (cloud account or sandbox).
- [ ] Prepare an API key with limited scope for hosted demo.
- [ ] Spin up a lightweight observability dashboard (Grafana template in repo).
- [ ] Validate the 3 test prompts and one long-run synthetic load for KV-cache exercise.

Workshop agenda (90 minutes recommended):
- 0–10 min: intro + success criteria with customer (latency < 200ms for interactive, cost target ~X tokens/1000).
- 10–30 min: quick on-hosted integration (demo app sends requests to Redwood API).
- 30–60 min: private/VPC skeleton deploy walkthrough (k8s manifest + helm).
- 60–80 min: performance experiments: batching vs no-batching, KV cache hit demo.
- 80–90 min: failure injection + fallback routing, wrap-up + next steps.

Prerequisites for customer participants:
- Laptop with Docker and kubectl; optionally cloud account if doing private deploy hands-on.
- A simple app repo clone (we provide a small Node+React microapp).

Core lab exercises (step-by-step rough notes):

Exercise 1 — Hosted API quickstart (10–20 min)
- Purpose: show app integration with minimal friction.
- Steps (SE-run or customer):
  1. Clone starter repo and open /examples/web-client.
  2. Set REDWOOD_API_KEY env var (use demo key).
  3. Run npm install && npm run dev.
  4. Send a sample chat request and inspect streaming tokens (demo shows partial tokens).
- Talking points: rate limiting, per-token cost view in console, streaming latency.

Mini snippet (JS example - present inline during workshop):
```js
const fetch = require('node-fetch');
async function generate(prompt) {
  const res = await fetch('https://api.redwood.ai/v1/generate', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Authorization': `Bearer ${process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY}`, 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ model: 'redwood-mini', input: prompt })
  });
  const json = await res.json();
  console.log(json.output);
}
```

Exercise 2 — Private/VPC skeleton deploy (30 min walkthrough, optional hands-on)
- Purpose: give customers a reproducible private deployment they can evaluate without full infra commitment. This is intentionally minimal: 1 control-plane, 1 inference pool (single GPU), basic KMS integration left as a stub.
- Files to highlight in repo:
  - k8s/redwood-controlplane.yaml (deployment + service)
  - k8s/inference-pool.yaml (nodeSelector, resources limits, tolerations)
  - helm/values-demo.yaml (image tags, model manifest override)
- Key steps (SE narrates):
  1. Apply manifests to a sandbox namespace: kubectl apply -f k8s/namespace.yaml && kubectl apply -f k8s/controlplane.yaml
  2. Port-forward control-plane to demo laptop: kubectl port-forward svc/redwood-controlplane 8080:80
  3. Start a minimal inference worker: kubectl apply -f k8s/inference-worker-demo.yaml
  4. Verify model is registered via control-plane /api/models endpoint.
- Troubleshooting notes:
  - If worker fails with OOM, lower batch_size in values-demo.yaml and restart.
  - If model fails to load, check image tags / quantized artifact mount path.

Exercise 2 snippet: kube manifest excerpt (show during walkthrough):
```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: redwood-inference-worker
spec:
  replicas: 1
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: worker
          image: redwood/worker:demo
          resources:
            limits:
              nvidia.com/gpu: "1"
          env:
            - name: MODEL_MANIFEST
              value: "/models/mini/model.json"
```

Exercise 3 — Batching, KV cache, and quick microbench (20–25 min)
- Purpose: tangible numbers customers can take away: per-token latency, tokens/sec, and effective cost impact from batching and KV cache.
- Steps:
  1. Run two workloads: single-request interactive vs batched 16 concurrent requests (script provided: scripts/microbench.py).
  2. Demonstrate prefix caching: send a repeated context (e.g., long system prompt) then subsequent calls should show cache hits in observability traces.
  3. Show token-level breakdown in console: model compute / queueing / network.
- Quick experiment results to reproduce during workshop (example numbers for demo):
  - Single interactive: 120ms median 1-token latency
  - Batched 16: 380ms end-to-end for whole batch, 24ms per token amortized
  - KV cache hit: 3x reduction in per-request compute for repeated prefixes

Microbench snippet (Python pseudo):
```py
import requests
for i in range(16):
    requests.post('http://localhost:8080/v1/generate', json={
        'model':'redwood-mini','input':'hello world', 'max_tokens':16
    })
```

Exercise 4 — Failure injection and graceful fallback routing (10–15 min)
- Purpose: show resilience features customers care about: model fallback, regional failover.
- Steps:
  1. In control-plane override route policy to point to a smaller model variant on capacity pressure.
  2. Simulate worker crash (kubectl scale deployment redwood-inference-worker --replicas=0).
  3. Observe automatic fallback to hosted variant (or to local smaller model) and demonstrate client behavior.
- Talking points: SLAs, choice of fallback strategies (cheapest/latency-optimized/identical-output), and how to configure automatic vs manual rollbacks.

Reference quick answers to anticipated questions:
- Q: How hard is it to replicate prod performance?
  A: This lab uses single-GPU and demo models. Production uses autoscaled pools, kernel selection, and CPU+GPU orchestration — we capture performance profiles in Redwood Console and can project expected throughput.
- Q: Will we lose prompts or data during fallback?
  A: Fallbacks can be configured with request-level retry & idempotency token; we preserve or synthesize best-effort responses depending on policy. We log all fallback events in audit traces for investigation.

SE notes / troubleshooting log (freeform, include during rehearsal):
- If control-plane health is flapping after restart: check leader-election annotations and shared storage mount.
- Common error: model artifact path mismatch (mount path in values-demo.yaml vs model manifest).
- Observability: if traces don’t correlate, ensure agent-side headers (x-request-id) are passed through reverse proxy.

Post-workshop deliverables (to attach to customer follow-up):
- Forked starter repo with customer-specific secrets redacted.
- Short slide with experiment numbers + recommended next steps (dedicated vs private sizing).
- Jira epic template to track pilot -> dedicated contract readiness (link in linked_artifacts).

Open questions to resolve before next workshop iteration:
- Can we streamline demo key issuance via a self-serve SE portal? (low priority)
- Add a 10–15 minute section specifically on quantized model artifacts and how they affect cold-start times.
- Improve the Grafana dashboard template to show KV-cache hit ratio prominently.

Appendix: quick checklist for SE day-of
- Bring: laptop, cloud sandbox creds (if private deploy), redwood demo key, HDMI for projector.
- Validate: repo builds locally, port-forwarding works, one GPU node available in sandbox.
- Ask customer up-front: what is their primary KPI (latency vs throughput vs cost) so we prioritize the right demos.

Comments: this is intentionally a low-friction lab that trades full production parity for speed-to-evidence. Keep the workshop conversational and adapt to the customer’s priorities.
